records.title: Probe several spots with a stick or stone
records.summary: Push a strong stick, a pointed stone or a hand tool into the ground at several spots to see whether the hard layer is the same everywhere or has softer, deeper pockets.
instructions: Pick at least five to ten spots spread across the area you might plant: high points, low points, near shrubs and near any trees.
At each spot, scrape away loose stones and dig or push down with a stick or pointed stone until it will not go further.
Measure each depth against your hand or forearm (for example: 'a hand deep', 'past my wrist', 'up to my elbow').
Mark the deepest spots with a stone or stick; these are the best places for planting pits.
Note whether the bottom feels like loose gravel you can scrape out or like a solid board of rock.
everyday_amounts: depth judged in hand-depths or forearm-lengths
limitations: A few holes cannot map the whole plateau; depth can change within a few paces.
A big stone can stop the stick even where soil is deeper beside it: try again a little to one side.
safety_notes: Do not force a tool through rock or jump on it; tools slip and break.
Do not dig near edges, drop-offs or under overhanging rock.
Wear something on your feet and keep hands clear of the stick tip.
records.purpose: Find out whether the hard layer is patchy (some spots can be deepened into pits) or one continuous sheet (build soil upward instead).

possible_outcomes.label: Depth changes from spot to spot
possible_outcomes.interpretation: The hard layer is patchy. Use the deeper spots for planting pits and build beds where it is shallow.

possible_outcomes.label: Stops at about the same shallow depth everywhere
possible_outcomes.interpretation: The hard layer is probably continuous. Do not keep digging; build soil upward with raised beds or containers and start with a small trial.

possible_outcomes.label: The stick goes down easily past the elbow in several spots
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Soil is deeper here than the typical plateau; pits will work well and roots have more room.

records.title: Hand-deep water-hole drainage check
records.summary: Dig a hole about a hand deep, fill it with water, and watch whether it drains away or just sits on the hard layer.
instructions: Dig a hole about a hand deep and a hand wide at a spot where you might plant.
Pour in water until it is full (half a bucket is usually plenty). Let it drain once to wet the sides.
Fill it again and watch. Check while you do other work, and again by evening.
Time the second filling in everyday terms: gone before you could sing a short song, gone within a few hours, or still there by morning.
If water is still standing the next morning, drainage is slow.
After a real rain, also look into any pits you dug: water still standing in them days later means slow drainage.
everyday_amounts: a hole about a hand deep and a hand wide
about half a bucket of water
limitations: One hole only tells you about that spot; repeat in two or three places if you can spare the water.
In the dry season the ground is very thirsty; the second filling is the one that counts.
safety_notes: If water is scarce, use dish or wash water rather than drinking water, or wait and look at pits after a rain.
Fill the hole back in or mark it so no one trips.
records.purpose: Learn whether water sinks away or sits on the hard layer, which decides between plain pits and raised beds or drained pits.

possible_outcomes.label: Second filling gone almost at once (before a short song ends)
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Very gravelly, leaky soil: water runs straight through. Hold moisture with plenty of compost, leaf litter and thick mulch.

possible_outcomes.label: Water is gone within a short while
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Water does not sit on the hard layer here. Pits are fine; mulch and organic matter are needed to hold moisture.

possible_outcomes.label: Water is still standing by evening or next morning
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Water sits on the hard layer. Prefer raised beds, or give pits an overflow notch and do not dig them where water collects.

records.title: Watch where the first heavy rain goes
records.summary: During or just after a heavy rain, watch from safe ground where water runs, where it pools and where it leaves the plateau.
instructions: From a safe spot, watch which way the water runs and mark the paths with sticks or stones afterwards.
Note low spots where water stands, and come back the next morning to see if it is still there.
Follow where the water leaves the plateau: never plan works that push it toward homes, paths, neighbours or crumbling edges.
Look for red streams, small channels and washed-out patches: these show where soil is being lost.
limitations: One storm can behave differently from the next; watch a second rain if you can.
safety_notes: Stay out of flowing water and away from channels and edges during storms.
Shelter from lightning; watch from cover or check the marks after the storm.
Never block or divert water toward homes, paths or neighbours' land.
records.purpose: Find the slope direction, the low spots where water pools, and the safe path for overflow before building stone lines or bunds.

possible_outcomes.label: Water runs off in one direction
possible_outcomes.interpretation: The ground slopes. Stone lines across the slope and half-moons can slow and catch this water.

possible_outcomes.label: Water stands in a few low spots
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Some pooling. Avoid planting in those spots or raise the planting there, and give water a safe way out.

possible_outcomes.label: Water stands over much of the area
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Widespread pooling on flat ground. Plant on raised beds and lead water away safely; do not build bunds that trap more water.

possible_outcomes.label: Water spreads thinly and does not stand anywhere
possible_outcomes.interpretation: No pooling seen. Mulch and small catchments around plants help more of it soak in.

records.title: Pour water to see the slope (dry-season check)
records.summary: Before the rains, pour a little water or roll a small round stone on bare ground to see which way the land falls.
instructions: Choose a bare, smooth patch. Pour a cup or two of water slowly and watch which way it trickles.
Repeat in a few places across the planting area.
Lay a stick in the direction the water ran: stone lines go across this direction, not along it.
If the water spreads in a puddle with no direction, the spot is flat and may pool in heavy rain.
everyday_amounts: a cup or two of water per spot
limitations: Small trickles show local slope only; watching a real rain is more reliable.
safety_notes: Do not do this near edges or drop-offs.
records.purpose: Find the direction of the slope without waiting for rain, so stone lines can be laid across it.

possible_outcomes.label: Water trickles one way
possible_outcomes.interpretation: There is a gentle slope; lay stone lines across it.

possible_outcomes.label: Water runs off quickly and the ground clearly drops away
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Steep ground: keep works small, keep away from edges.

possible_outcomes.label: Water spreads and stays
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Flat spot: water may pool here in heavy rain.

records.title: Baking-soda fizz check (weak clue only)
records.summary: Mix a pinch of baking soda into a spoonful of wet soil and look for fizzing. This is a weak hint, not a soil test.
instructions: Take a spoonful of soil from the root zone, remove stones, and wet it into a mud with clean water.
Sprinkle a pinch of baking soda on top and watch and listen closely.
Note whether you see any fizzing or bubbles.
Whatever happens, keep planning for acidic, poor soil: add organic matter and choose tolerant crops.
limitations: Weak evidence only: not a measurement and not a substitute for a soil test.
No fizz does not prove the soil is not acidic.
Results depend on water, soil moisture and how fresh the baking soda is.
Never required before planting; repeating it after treatment is an optional clue only.
safety_notes: Keep baking soda and soil out of eyes and mouth; wash hands after.
records.purpose: Give a rough, optional hint about acidity when nothing else is available. It never decides the plan.

possible_outcomes.label: Some fizzing or bubbles
possible_outcomes.interpretation: A weak hint that the soil may be acidic. It does not tell you how acidic, and it does not change the basic plan.

possible_outcomes.label: No fizzing
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Proves nothing: many acidic soils show no fizz with this check. Keep treating the soil as likely acidic and poor.

records.title: Look for rusty rock lumps and ironstone gravel
records.summary: Look at the surface and at the soil you dug out: heavy, rusty lumps and pea-sized gravel are hardened iron-rich material typical of laterite.
instructions: Pick up a few stones: laterite pieces are often rusty-red to dark brown, heavy for their size, and sometimes full of small holes.
In each dug hole, scrape the bottom: does it come away as loose gravel, or is it one welded hard surface?
Look at edges of channels or cuttings where the layer may show in side view.
Collect loose lumps for stone lines and half-moon edges.
limitations: Colour and weight are clues; they do not show how thick the layer is.
safety_notes: Lift stones with bent knees; watch for snakes and scorpions under them.
records.purpose: Recognise laterite and judge whether the hard layer is loose gravel you can scrape out or a welded sheet.

possible_outcomes.label: Bottom scrapes out as loose gravel
possible_outcomes.interpretation: The hard layer is broken or gravelly here; with effort, pits can be deepened a little in these spots.

possible_outcomes.label: Bottom is one welded rock surface wherever you dig
possible_outcomes.interpretation: A continuous sheet. Do not try to break it; build upward.

possible_outcomes.label: Rusty lumps scattered on the surface
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Confirms laterite-type ground and gives you stone for lines.

records.title: Ask neighbours what survives and when rains reliably start
records.summary: Ask anyone who has lived here what grows through the dry season, when the soaking rains usually begin, and how long they last.
instructions: Ask: which plants survive the long dry season here, and which crops have people tried?
Ask: when do the rains usually become reliable (not just the first storm), and roughly how many weeks do they last?
Ask: has anyone tried pits, beds or stone lines here, and what happened?
Write down what you hear. Treat each claim as something to test with a small trial, not as a fact.
If local advice says 'only trees grow here', ask why: is it the hard layer, the water, animals, or that nobody tried?
limitations: Memories of rain timing are rough and seasons vary year to year.
Local advice can be right for reasons you cannot see, or outdated; it is weighed, not obeyed.
safety_notes: Respect other people's land and water sources.
records.purpose: Gather local knowledge as a clue to verify: crop experience, rain timing and season length.

possible_outcomes.label: Locals say only tree crops grow here
possible_outcomes.interpretation: A claim to check. It may reflect the hard layer; a small trial of pits or beds with short-season crops can test it while tree options are planned too.

possible_outcomes.label: Locals give other advice (crops, timing, methods)
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Useful clues; compare them with your own observations and test on a small plot.

possible_outcomes.label: No one to ask
possible_outcomes.interpretation: No local advice; rely on careful observation, short-season crops and a small trial.

records.title: Inventory what you have
records.summary: Walk around and list what can be gathered or used: organic matter, mulch, stones, ash, shells, containers, seeds and tools.
instructions: Count buckets or containers that can hold water, and any sheet, tarp or roof that could catch rain.
Look for organic matter: compost, manure, fallen leaves, dry grass, shrub prunings, crop residues, kitchen scraps.
Look for loose stones you can carry for stone lines.
Check for wood ash from cooking fires and any shells (egg, snail).
Check seeds: what kinds, how many handfuls, and whether they look healthy and dry.
List tools: stick, hoe, spade, machete, bucket.
limitations: Gathering takes time; plan the work around the weeks left before the rains.
safety_notes: Do not take materials from other people's land or fields without asking.
records.purpose: Match the plan to real resources and choose alternatives where something is missing.

possible_outcomes.label: Compost or manure available
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Use it to fill pits and beds.

possible_outcomes.label: No compost or manure
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Use leaf litter, dry grass, prunings and residues instead; start sheet composting.

possible_outcomes.label: Water containers available
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Set them up to catch rain before the season.

possible_outcomes.label: Little or no stored water
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Favour drought-hardy crops, mulch heavily and capture rain.

possible_outcomes.label: Plenty of loose stones
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Build stone lines across the slope.

possible_outcomes.label: Wood ash available
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Optional small handful per pit only, with care.

possible_outcomes.label: Seeds available
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Choose crops from what you have that suit the soil and season.

records.title: Read the plants that already grow here
records.summary: Look at what grows naturally and where: tufted dry grass, thorny shrubs, trees, greener patches. Plants are clues, not proof.
instructions: Note where shrubs or trees grow: they often mark cracks or pockets of deeper soil.
Look for greener patches in dips after rain: water may collect there.
Look at grass: dry tufts with bare ground between suggest shallow, droughty soil.
Mark promising spots for pits or a trial plot.
limitations: Wild plants tolerate conditions crops may not; grazing and fire also shape what grows.
safety_notes: Beware of thorns, snakes and stinging insects in shrubs.
records.purpose: Spot deeper or moister pockets and get a rough idea of how harsh the ground is.

possible_outcomes.label: Dry tufts and thorny shrubs only
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Typical of shallow, droughty laterite: plan for very poor soil and short-season crops.

possible_outcomes.label: Some trees survive the dry season
possible_outcomes.interpretation: There may be deeper pockets near them; tree crops might be possible in enlarged pits there.

possible_outcomes.label: Greener patches in low spots
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Water collects there. Good for moisture but watch for waterlogging after heavy rain.

records.title: Check how deep the rain has soaked
records.summary: After a rain, dig a small hole beside a planting spot with a stick to see whether the soil is moist all the way down to the hard layer.
instructions: The day after a rain, dig a small hole with a stick or fingers beside a pit or bed.
Feel the soil: is it moist and darker all the way down to the hard layer, or only a thin wet skin over dry soil?
Squeeze a pinch: moist soil holds together briefly; dry soil runs through your fingers.
Sow only after this has happened after more than one rain, with no long dry gap in between.
everyday_amounts: a pinch of soil squeezed between fingers
limitations: Rain can still stop for a while after it starts; watching neighbours' timing helps.
safety_notes: Refill the small hole after checking.
records.purpose: Decide whether the rains are reliable enough to sow (soil moist down to the hard layer after more than one soaking rain).

possible_outcomes.label: Moist all the way down to the hard layer
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Soil is soaked. If this has happened after more than one rain, conditions are right to sow.

possible_outcomes.label: Only a thin wet skin; dry below
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Most of the rain ran off. Wait for more rain, and improve catchment (mulch, half-moons, stone lines).

records.title: Watch how trial plants grow
records.summary: Compare plants in the trial plot over the first weeks: colour, size, and how they cope with dry days.
instructions: Every few days, look at leaf colour, plant size and how many seedlings survive in each pit or bed.
Pale or yellowing older leaves, purplish tints or stunted plants can point to hungry, acidic soil.
Compare spots with more compost or mulch against spots with less.
Write down what you see in the journal and adjust: more organic matter, more mulch, different crop.
limitations: Pests, heat and dry spells also cause yellowing or stunting; look at the whole picture.
safety_notes: Wash hands after handling plants with signs of disease.
records.purpose: Use the crop itself as the best available sign of soil fertility and acidity stress, since there is no lab.

possible_outcomes.label: Plants green and growing evenly
possible_outcomes.interpretation: The pit or bed fill is working; expand gradually.

possible_outcomes.label: Pale, yellowing or stunted plants
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Likely hunger and acidity stress. Add compost or manure top-ups and more mulch; consider tougher crops.

possible_outcomes.label: Plants wilt fast in dry spells
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Soil holds little water: deepen mulch, use stored water, shade seedlings.

records.title: Seed sprout test
records.summary: Before sowing, sprout a few seeds of each kind on a damp cloth to see how many are alive, then decide how many seeds to sow per spot.
instructions: Count out ten seeds of one kind.
Lay them on a damp cloth or paper, fold it over, and keep it damp and warm in the shade.
Look each day for a few days (small seeds sprout faster than big ones).
Count how many have put out a little root.
Repeat for each kind of seed you plan to sow.
limitations: Seed in the soil faces heat, dryness and pests, so field sprouting is usually lower than on the cloth.
safety_notes: Never eat seed that has been chemically treated (often coloured).
records.purpose: Avoid wasting a sowing on dead seed, and set the number of seeds per spot from what actually sprouts.

possible_outcomes.label: Most sprout (about seven or more of ten)
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Seed is good: sow the usual pinch per spot.

possible_outcomes.label: About half sprout
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Seed is weak: sow about twice as many seeds per spot and keep extra back for re-sowing.

possible_outcomes.label: Few or none sprout
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Do not rely on this seed. Find fresher seed from neighbours or a market; eat the rest if it is safe food grain.

records.title: Float seed test (weak clue)
records.summary: Drop seeds into a bowl of water: seeds that float are often empty or old. A quick weak clue; the sprout test is more reliable.
instructions: Drop a handful of seed into a bowl of clean water and stir.
Wait a short while and skim off the seeds that float.
Dry the sinkers in shade before sowing or storing again.
limitations: Weak clue only: some good seeds float and some dead seeds sink; it does not work well for very light seeds.
safety_notes: Do not soak treated seed in water you will drink or cook with.
records.purpose: Quickly sort out obviously empty seed before sowing.

possible_outcomes.label: Most seeds sink
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Probably filled seed; confirm with the sprout test if unsure.

possible_outcomes.label: Many seeds float
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Much of the seed may be empty or old; do a sprout test and find better seed if possible.

records.title: Life count: worms and small creatures in a handful
records.summary: Dig out a few handfuls of soil, spread them on a cloth, and count the worms, beetles and other small creatures you see.
instructions: Dig a small hole about a hand deep and spread the soil on a cloth or sack.
Sift through it with your fingers for a short while and count worms, beetles, ants and grubs.
Do the same in a mulched, composted pit after some weeks of rain and compare.
everyday_amounts: a hole about a hand deep
limitations: Dry-season soil shows little life even when it is recovering; compare at similar moisture.
safety_notes: Watch for scorpions and stinging ants; use a stick to spread the soil.
records.purpose: Get a rough sign of soil life before and after adding organic matter and mulch.

possible_outcomes.label: Almost nothing living
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Soil life is very low: add compost or organic matter and keep it covered with mulch.

possible_outcomes.label: Several worms or creatures
possible_outcomes.interpretation: Soil life is present; the organic matter and mulch are working.
